description: Interactive step-based number line explorer for Grade 7 Mathematics — Jump Jackpot HCF Discovery. A horizontal number line from 0 to 35 with two treasure chest icons at configurable positions. A frog character (Jumpy) hops forward from 0 in equal-sized jumps, landing positions highlighted with coloured dots. Green dots when landing on a treasure, red dots otherwise. Each step tests a different jump size with smooth hop animations. A verdict table grows on the right side, recording each jump size and whether it hit both treasures. Final reveal shows the HCF with a golden highlight. Indian school context — treasure chests styled with Diwali lantern colours. Clean educational design with Lily Script One and Nunito font families. Touch-friendly controls for mobile use. 5-colour palette: indigo (#6366f1) for jumps, emerald (#10b981) for hits, rose (#f43f5e) for misses, white background, dark slate (#1e293b) text.
subject: Mathematics
topic: Jump Jackpot Game — HCF as Longest Jump Size
learningObjectives: Understand that a jump size must be a common factor of both treasure positions to land on both
Discover that the longest working jump size equals the HCF of the two numbers
Visualize factors and common factors on a number line
Connect the Jump Jackpot game to the concept of Highest Common Factor (HCF / GCD)

structure.description: Final reveal — shows that the longest working jump = HCF of the two numbers

teachingNotes.step1: Show the number line with two treasures at the configured positions (default: 14 and 30). Ask the student what jump sizes they think would work.
teachingNotes.step2: Try the first jump size — observe which treasures it hits or misses. Ask why it fails for the one(s) it misses (the treasure position is not a multiple of the jump size).
teachingNotes.step3: Continue through each trial jump size. For each, ask: Is this number a factor of BOTH treasure positions?
teachingNotes.step4: After all trials, reveal the verdict table. The longest jump that hits both = HCF.
teachingNotes.step5: Ask: Why must the jump size be a COMMON FACTOR of both numbers? Because Jumpy lands only on multiples of the jump size, so both treasure positions must be multiples.
teachingNotes.step6: Connect to formal definition: HCF (Highest Common Factor) = Greatest Common Divisor (GCD).

instructionsForStudent: Watch the number line as Jumpy tries different jump sizes. For each jump size, check whether Jumpy lands on BOTH treasure numbers. Keep track of which sizes work and which do not in the verdict table on the right. The longest jump size that hits both treasures is a special number — can you guess what it is before the reveal? Hint: Think about factors!
